Veil of the Temple
VAYL of the TEM-pul
n. phrase
Veil from Latin velum, “covering, sail.” Hebrew pārōcheth, the inner curtain separating the holy place from the most holy place in the tabernacle and temple; Greek katapetasma, the same.

Biblical Definition

The Veil of the Temple was the inner curtain separating the holy place from the most holy place in the tabernacle and (subsequently) the temple—a heavy embroidered curtain of blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen, with cherubim wrought into it, hung on pillars of shittim wood overlaid with gold. Exodus 26:31-34 prescribes its construction. The veil’s primary function was to divide—to mark the boundary between the holy place (where the priests ministered daily) and the most holy place (where God’s presence dwelt above the mercy seat, and where only the high priest could enter, only once a year, on the Day of Atonement, with the blood of atonement). The veil therefore stood as the visible architectural confession of the sinful creature’s exclusion from the holy God’s immediate presence: God dwelt in unapproachable light; the veil hung between Him and His people; only the appointed priest could pass through, only by the appointed blood, only on the appointed day. The supreme moment of biblical history with respect to the veil is at the death of Christ. Matthew 27:50-51, Mark 15:37-38, Luke 23:45-46: at the moment of Christ’s death, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent. The detail is structurally significant. The veil was rent from the top to the bottom: not by human hands (which would have torn it from the bottom up), but by divine action from above, marking that the rending was God’s own work and not man’s. The timing was at the moment of Christ’s death: the architectural confession of the New Covenant reality, that the way into the holiest is now made manifest by the death of the Mediator. Hebrews 10:19-22 makes the doctrine explicit: having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, By a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh; And having an high priest over the house of God; Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water. The veil was Christ’s flesh; the rending of the veil at His death was the opening of the new and living way through which every saint now has boldness of access to the holiest. The doctrine is therefore central to the New Covenant. The barrier between sinners and the holy God—real, prescribed, enforced under death in the Old Covenant—has been removed by the death of Christ. The way into the holiest is open. The saint draws near with boldness, by the blood of Jesus, through the rent veil of His flesh, into the very presence of God where the high priest of the Old Covenant could enter only once a year.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines VEIL as a cover; a curtain; a piece of cloth used to hide something; in scripture, the inner curtain of the tabernacle and temple separating the holy place from the most holy; rent at Christ’s death from top to bottom, opening the new and living way of access to the holiest by His blood.

expand to see more

VEIL, n. — A cover; a curtain; something to intercept the view, and hide an object. In scripture, the inner curtain of the tabernacle and temple, dividing the holy place from the most holy. Made of blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen, with cherubim wrought thereon (Ex 26:31).

TEMPLE, n. — A house dedicated to the worship of some deity. In scripture, the building at Jerusalem in which the Jews worshipped God before its destruction in AD 70.

Key Scripture

Matthew 27:50-51 — "Jesus, when he had cried again with a loud voice, yielded up the ghost. And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent."

Hebrews 10:19-22 — "Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, By a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh; And having an high priest over the house of God; Let us draw near..."

Exodus 26:31-33 — "And thou shalt make a veil of blue, and purple, and scarlet, and fine twined linen of cunning work: with cherubims shall it be made: And thou shalt hang it upon four pillars of shittim wood overlaid with gold... And the veil shall divide unto you between the holy place and the most holy."

Hebrews 6:19-20 — "Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil; Whither the forerunner is for us entered, even Jesus, made an high priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec."

Modern Corruption

The veil-of-the-temple doctrine is corrupted, in much contemporary preaching, by the muting of its architectural-confessional substance (the real exclusion of sinners from God’s presence under the Old Covenant) and the consequent muting of the cross-event of the rent veil (the real opening of the new and living way at Christ’s death)—and by the inverse over-spiritualization that detaches the doctrine from its historical-architectural reality.

expand to see more

Much contemporary preaching has muted both ends of the veil-doctrine. The Old Covenant’s real exclusion of sinners from the holy place is rarely preached: the veil is treated as ancient symbol rather than as the architectural confession that the sinful creature was, in fact, kept from the holy God’s immediate presence on pain of death. And the cross-event of the rent veil is correspondingly muted: the structural significance of the curtain being torn from top to bottom at the moment of Christ’s death is mentioned briefly if at all, without the substantive doctrine that the new and living way has been opened. The recovery is the recovery of both ends. The Old Covenant exclusion was real: the holy God dwelt in unapproachable light; the veil really divided; only the high priest, only once a year, only by appointed blood could pass through. The cross-event was correspondingly real: at the moment Christ died, God Himself tore the veil from above, signaling that the way is now open through the rent body of His Son. The two together form the deep architectural-and-Christological substance of Hebrews 10:19-22’s great application: let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith.

The opposite corruption is the over-spiritualization that detaches the doctrine from its historical-architectural reality. Some readings treat the veil as merely symbolic from the start, with the historical curtain in the historical temple having no real substantive role beyond illustrating the spiritual exclusion. The biblical pattern refuses this. The Old Testament veil was a real curtain in a real building, prescribed in detail by the LORD Himself; the Day of Atonement was a real annual ritual in which a real high priest passed through a real veil with real blood; the rending of the veil at Christ’s death was a real event in real history, observed by real witnesses (the Synoptic Gospels uniformly record it). The architectural reality grounds the spiritual substance. Where the architectural reality is treated as mere illustration, the spiritual substance becomes vague; where the architectural reality is honored as the appointed shadow, the spiritual substance shines through with full force. Recover both. The Old Covenant exclusion was architecturally enforced; the cross opened the way architecturally and substantively; the saint now draws near with boldness through the rent veil of Christ’s flesh, into the very holiest of the holies, where the Father waits to receive His children through the high priest who has opened the way.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pārōcheth; Greek katapetasma; the inner curtain of tabernacle and temple separating the holy place from the most holy; rent from top to bottom at Christ’s death, fulfilling the architectural confession of Old Covenant exclusion in the opening of the new and living way to the holiest by His blood (Heb 10:19-22).

expand to see more

Hebrew pārōcheth (H6532) — veil, inner curtain (25 OT uses).

Greek katapetasma (G2665) — veil, curtain (6 NT uses; Matt 27:51; Mark 15:38; Luke 23:45; Heb 6:19; 9:3; 10:20).

Hebrew māsāk (H4539) — screen, covering (the outer curtain at the entrance of the tent of meeting, distinct from the inner veil).

Greek schizō (G4977) — to split, tear (the verb of the veil’s rending at Matt 27:51).

Usage

"The veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom—the rending was God’s own action from above, not man’s."

"The veil was Christ’s flesh (Heb 10:20); the rending opened the new and living way of access to the holiest by His blood."

"Muted preaching loses the Old Covenant exclusion and the cross-event together; over-spiritualization detaches the doctrine from historical reality; biblical doctrine holds the architectural confession and the cross-event together as Hebrews 10:19-22 sets them."
